questions.text: 'Most powerful weapon of the Spanish conqueror was not a conventional military weapon at all.' Justify the statement by giving two reasons.
questions.answer:
1. They used germs like smallpox, which spread deep into the continent before any European could reach there.
2. America's original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases that came from Europe. The disease wiped out whole communities, leading to conquest. This biological warfare in the mid sixteenth century made it easy for the Spanish to overpower the Americans.

questions.text: 'The female figures become an allegory of the nation during the 19th century in Europe.' Elaborate on the statement with examples.
questions.answer:
1. Artists wanted to personify the nation. Nations were represented as female figures; the female form did not belong to any particular woman in real life but was an abstract idea that gave the nation a concrete form.
2. The female figure became an allegory of France, named Marianne, representing the nation. Her characteristics - red cap, tricolour and cockade - were drawn from those of Liberty and the Republic.
3. Similarly, Germania became the allegory of the German nation. Germania wears a crown of oak leaves because oak stands for heroism.

or.text: Assess the role of the Greek War of Independence in shaping nationalist consciousness among educated Europeans in the nineteenth century.
or.answer:
1. Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century. The growth of revolutionary nationalism in Europe sparked off a struggle for independence amongst the Greeks which began in 1821.
2. Nationalists in Greece got support from other Greeks living in exile and from many West Europeans who had sympathies for ancient Greek culture. Poets and artists lauded Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion to support its struggle against a Muslim empire.
3. The English poet Lord Byron organised funds and later went to fight in the war, where he died of fever in 1824. Finally, the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation.

questions.text: Evaluate the economic consequences of the Non-Cooperation Movement for colonial rule in India.
questions.answer:
1. The effects of non-cooperation on the economic front were more dramatic. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed, and foreign cloth burnt in huge bonfires.
2. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.
3. In many places merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or finance foreign trade.
4. As the boycott movement spread, people began discarding imported clothes and wearing only Indian ones.
5. Production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up and making and wearing of Khadi became very popular.

or.text: Analyse how Indian merchants and industrialists associated themselves with the Civil Disobedience Movement, highlighting the forms of support they extended and the reasons for their participation.
or.answer:
1. During the First World War, Indian merchants and industrialists had made huge profits and become powerful. Keen on expanding their business, they reacted against colonial policies that restricted business activities.
2. They wanted protection against imports of foreign goods, and a rupee-sterling foreign exchange ratio that would discourage imports.
3. To organise business interests, they formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927. Led by industrialists like Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, they attacked colonial control over the Indian economy and supported the Civil Disobedience Movement when it was first launched.
4. They gave financial assistance and refused to buy or sell imported goods. Most businessmen came to see swaraj as a time when colonial restrictions on business would no longer exist.
5. But after the failure of the Round Table Conference, business groups were no longer uniformly enthusiastic; they were apprehensive of militant activities, prolonged disruption of business and the growing influence of socialism among younger Congress members.

questions.text:
Read the following text and answer the questions that follow:
Print comes to India
The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed several tracts. By 1674, about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kanara languages. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book was printed by them. By 1710, Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts, many of them translations of older works.
The English language press did not grow in India till quite late. From 1780, James Augustus Hickey edited the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine that claimed to be independent of colonial influence. This marked the beginning of English newspaper printing in India.
Source-India and the Contemporary World - II, NCERT. Class 10, Chapter 5

subparts.text: Identify the newspaper that marked the beginning of English newspaper printing in India.
Explain how James Augustus Hickey demonstrated independence through his newspaper.
subparts.answer: He published a private weekly newspaper that claimed to be open to all and not influenced by colonial authorities.

subparts.text: Evaluate how the early printing activities contributed to the spread of knowledge in India before English newspapers became popular.
subparts.answer: Early printing helped spread knowledge by printing books and religious texts in regional languages such as Konkani, Tamil and Malayalam. This made written material accessible to local people and encouraged the circulation of ideas much before the rise of English newspapers.

questions.text: A drought-prone district wants to adopt a sustainable water conservation method using traditional knowledge. Suggest two suitable rainwater harvesting practices that could be implemented.
questions.answer:
1. Rooftop rainwater harvesting: rainwater collected from rooftops is stored in tanks for domestic use, helping reduce dependence on surface and groundwater sources during dry periods.
2. Johads or khadins: these structures store rainwater and allow it to seep into the ground, which helps recharge groundwater and supports irrigation in water-scarce areas.

questions.text: A farmer plans to shift from food crops to plantation crops and is to choose between tea and coffee. Highlight the difference in the conditions associated with their growth.
questions.answer:
- Tea is more suitable in areas with high rainfall distributed throughout the year, unlike coffee which prefers seasonal rainfall.
- Tea requires a frost-free climate, making it ideal for tropical and sub-tropical regions.
- Coffee (Arabica) is suitable for regions with moderate temperatures and well-drained slopes, such as the Western Ghats.
- Tea plantations demand large-scale labour availability, while coffee requires comparatively less labour.
- Coffee cultivation is geographically more restricted, whereas tea can be grown in several regions of India.

or.text: Farmers in a region experiencing moderate rainfall, cool winters, and assured irrigation plan to move from mixed cropping to the cultivation of a single cereal crop. Should they opt for rice or wheat? Support your answer with appropriate reasons based on crop requirements.
or.answer:
Wheat should be chosen.
- Wheat is more suitable as it grows well in cool temperatures during the growing season.
- The region's moderate rainfall matches wheat's requirement of 50-75 cm.
- Wheat requires bright sunshine at the time of ripening, which is common in winter months.
- Availability of irrigation supports wheat cultivation in areas with limited rainfall.
- Wheat is traditionally grown in north and north-western regions, matching the given conditions.

questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Role of Communities in Forest Conservation
In many parts of India, especially in tribal and mountainous regions, local communities depend on forests for fuel, fodder, and livelihood. Over time, people realised that uncontrolled exploitation by contractors and commercial interests was destroying forests and threatening their survival. This led to community-led conservation efforts where people actively protected forests through traditional practices and movements. One such movement began in the Himalayan region, where villagers protected trees by hugging them, highlighting the importance of people's participation in conservation.
Source- Contemporary India - II, NCERT, Chapter 2

subparts.text: State any one objective of community-based forest conservation.
subparts.answer: To ensure the protection and sustainable use of forest resources by involving local communities.

subparts.text: How does people's participation lead to more effective forest resource management? Elaborate with the help of two examples.
subparts.answer:
- Local communities possess traditional knowledge of forests, which helps in their sustainable management.
- People develop a sense of responsibility and ownership, preventing over-exploitation of resources.
Examples (any 2): farmers and citizens' groups like the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that adequate levels of diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals are possible and economically viable; Joint Forest Management (JFM), where local communities and the government jointly manage forest resources. (Or any other relevant example.)

questions.text: How the powers were shared between the central and state government in Belgium to avoid the division of the country? Explain.
questions.answer:
(Any 2 points)
1. The Constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers shall be equal in the central government.
2. Many powers of the Central government have been given to the State governments of the two regions. The State governments are not subordinate to the Central government.
3. Brussels has a separate government in which both communities have equal representation.

questions.text: Why is a democratic system of government regarded as the best form of governance in terms of involving the maximum number of citizens as stakeholders in political power? Explain with suitable arguments.
questions.answer:
(Any 2 points)
1. People as the source of political power - in a democracy the people are the ultimate source of all political power; they have the right and opportunity to participate in governing themselves through institutions of self-government.
2. Active participation and representation - citizens actively participate in political processes, have representation in government and get opportunities to take part in decision-making.
3. Accountability and stability - democracy encourages public debate and expression of opinion, which influence policy making; it allows people to hold the government accountable, ensures transparency, reduces conflicts between social groups and gives legitimacy to the elected government, contributing to political stability.

questions.text: The focus on caste in politics can sometimes give an impression that elections are all about caste and nothing else. However, that is far from true. Analyze this statement by giving three valid arguments.
questions.answer:
(Any 3 points)
1. No parliamentary constituency in the country has a clear majority of one single caste, so every candidate and party needs to win the confidence of more than one caste and community.
2. No party wins the votes of all the voters of a caste or community. When a caste is called a 'vote bank' of one party, it usually means a large proportion of the voters of that caste vote for that party.
3. Many political parties may put up candidates from the same caste (if that caste is believed to dominate the electorate in a constituency). Some voters have more than one candidate from their caste while many have no candidate from their caste.
4. The ruling party and the sitting MP or MLA frequently lose elections in our country; that could not happen if all castes and communities were frozen in their political preferences.

questions.text: Explain any five provisions of the constitutional amendments of 1992 which strengthened the third tier of democracy in India?
questions.answer:
1. It is now constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections to local government bodies.
2. Seats are reserved in the elected bodies and the executive heads of these institutions for the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.
3. At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women.
4. An independent institution called the State Election Commission has been created in each State to conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
5. The State governments are required to share some powers and revenue with local government bodies. The nature of sharing varies from State to State.

or.text: 'The Constitution declared India as a Union of States. Although it did not use the word federation, the Indian Union is based on the principles of federalism.' What makes India a federal country?
or.answer:
(Any 5 points)
1. Division of powers - the Constitution divides powers between the Union Government and State Governments through three lists: Union List, State List and Concurrent List.
2. Written and supreme Constitution - all governments must function within its limits; the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.
3. Rigidity of the Constitution - the division of powers cannot be changed easily; any amendment affecting the federal structure requires approval of both Parliament and State Legislatures.
4. Independent judiciary - the Supreme Court is an impartial authority that settles disputes between the Centre and States and protects the Constitution.
5. Dual government system - there are two levels of government: the Central Government for the whole country and State Governments for their respective states.
6. Financial autonomy - States have their own sources of revenue, though some taxes are shared with the Centre.

questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Need for political parties
Political parties are easily one of the most visible institutions in a democracy. For most ordinary citizens, democracy is equal to political parties. If you travel to remote parts of our country and speak to the less educated citizens, you could come across people who may not know anything about our Constitution or about the nature of our government. But chances are that they would know something about our political parties. At the same time, this visibility does not mean popularity. Most people tend to be very critical of political parties. They tend to blame parties for all that is wrong with our democracy and our political life. Parties have become identified with social and political divisions. Therefore, it is natural to ask if we need political parties at all? About a hundred years ago, there were few countries in the world that had any political party. Now there are few that do not have parties.
Source- NCERT. Democratic Politics-II. Class X

subparts.text: Modern democracies cannot exist without political parties. Analyse the given statement by giving one reason to support your answer.
subparts.answer: (Any one) Without parties every candidate in the elections would be independent, so no one would be able to make promises to the people about any major policy changes. The government may be formed, but its utility would remain uncertain; elected representatives would be accountable to their constituency only for what they do in their locality.

subparts.text: Highlight any two functions of a political party.
subparts.answer: (Any 2) Contesting elections; formulating policies and programmes; making laws; forming and running governments; playing the role of opposition; shaping public opinion; providing access to government machinery and welfare schemes.

subparts.text: Why has India opted for a Multi-Party System? Give any one reason to support your answer.
subparts.answer: India adopted a multi-party system mainly because of its vast social and geographical diversity (religions, cultures, languages, regions), which could not be adequately represented by one or two parties; it ensures a broader voice and prevents concentration of power in a single group.

questions.text: Ravi noticed that in many villages of India, more people are working on farms than actually needed, and yet many of them do not get proper wages or regular work. What could be the reason behind such a situation? Suggest any two ways to tackle this problem effectively. (1+2=3)
questions.answer:
This is called disguised unemployment. Causes (any 1): excess labour in agriculture; lack of alternative employment opportunities; poverty and population pressure; lack of skills and training required for other kinds of work.
Solutions (any 2): diversification of activities - introduce other rural jobs like small-scale industries, dairy and poultry farming; land reforms and consolidation - combine small plots so fewer workers are underemployed; skill development and education - train people for non-agricultural jobs in towns or industries to reduce surplus labour on farms.

questions.text: Explain how Self-Help Groups (SHGs) help banks to minimize risk when providing loans to poor women, who do not have any collateral.
questions.answer:
(Any 3)
- SHG members are collectively responsible for repayment, so banks have assurance of repayment.
- The group monitors individual members and follows up on non-repayment cases.
- Regular savings and organised meetings show discipline and reliability, making banks confident to lend.

questions.text: Improvements in technology and liberalization together have accelerated globalization. Evaluate.
questions.answer:
1. Technology (transport, telecom, Internet) allows fast movement of goods, services and information across countries.
2. Liberalisation reduces trade barriers and allows foreign investments, making it easier for businesses to operate globally.
3. Together, they increase interconnection between countries, integrate markets and expand opportunities for trade and investment.

questions.text:
While studying the table given below for their Social Science project, two classmates A and B, notice significant differences in the Literacy Rate and Infant Mortality Rate while comparing the development indicators of three states. Analyse how the development levels of these states differ and suggest the inferences A and B can draw. What areas should each state focus on to improve their overall development? (1+2+2=5)

Table: Comparison of Development Indicators

| State | Infant Mortality Rate (per 1,000 live births) (2020) | Literacy Rate (%) (2017-18) | Net Attendance Ratio (Secondary Stage) (%) 2017-18 |
|---|---|---|---|
| H | 28 | 82 | 73 |
| K | 6 | 94 | 94 |
| B | 27 | 62 | 69 |

Adapted from - Sources: Economic Survey 2023-24, National Sample Survey Organisation (Report No. 585), National Statistical Office, Government of India; National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) 2019-21 IIPS, Mumbai.
questions.answer:
(The marking scheme reads the states as Haryana = H, Kerala = K, Bihar = B.)
Analysis: Kerala performs best on both indicators (highest literacy and lowest infant mortality), Bihar performs weakest, and Haryana lies in between with moderate literacy but a high infant mortality rate.
Inferences (any 2): higher literacy seems linked with better health outcomes (Kerala: literacy 94%, IMR 6; Bihar: literacy 62%, IMR 27, indicating limited access to quality education and healthcare); Kerala's performance shows long-term social investment in education and public health pays off; the wide gaps show that development in India is uneven and depends on policies, governance quality and resource allocation.
Suggestions (any 2): Haryana should improve maternal and child healthcare to reduce its high IMR while strengthening education quality; Bihar needs to prioritise both expanding literacy and improving basic health facilities; Kerala should maintain and further strengthen its existing education and healthcare systems.

or.text:
Study the table given above and answer:
Which of the three states is likely to have a better human development standard than the others? Justify explaining any two reasons for your answer. Why is it important to pay attention to indicators like Infant Mortality Rate (IMR), Literacy Rate, and Net Attendance Ratio to bring about an overall development of any state. (1+2+2=5)
or.answer:
Kerala (K) is likely to have a better human development standard than Haryana and Bihar.
Reasons (any 2): (1) low Infant Mortality Rate (6) - the lowest number of children dying before age one, showing strong healthcare; (2) high literacy rate (94%) and Net Attendance Ratio (94%) - most people can read and write and most children attend secondary school, reflecting good education and social development.
Importance (any 2): IMR - reducing infant deaths ensures healthier children and a stronger, more productive population; Literacy Rate and Net Attendance Ratio - education empowers people and improves awareness of health, employment and civic responsibilities, leading to overall development of the state.
